# R18.6: China AI Open Source Ecosystem Blue Book/Blue Paper (English edition): extraction notes

Source files: `scratchpad/kys-read/bluebook/00…08-*.md` (~22.4k words). All files read in full.
Companion table: `out/18.6-bluebook-claims.tsv` (156 rows). Quotes are verbatim with markdown emphasis and escapes removed. 149 were checked automatically against the source. The other 7 come from wrapped grid-table cells and were checked by hand.

## 0. Provenance warning (read first)

The English text does **not** match the brief "KAIYUANSHE, published 8 Nov 2026":
- Title page: "**China AI Open Source Ecosystem Blue Paper**", "**Datawhale AI Industry Research Institute**", "**March 2026**" (stated twice).
- "Published by": **Hangzhou AI Open Source Ecosystem Academy** (logo file `hangzhoushirengongzhinengkaiyuanshengtaixueyuan.jpg`). Co-publishers appear only as one logo image (`unify-logos.png`) and cannot be read from the text.
- KAIYUANSHE (开源社) is **not named anywhere** in the text. The latest "accessed" date in the references is 19 March 2026.
- Before citing, re-attribute it as: Datawhale AI Industry Research Institute / Hangzhou AI Open Source Ecosystem Academy (Mar 2026). The 8 Nov 2026 date could belong to a later KAIYUANSHE re-release or the Chinese edition. Check the cover/colophon of the Chinese PDF.

## 2. Structure and argument (≤300 words)

The book is a policy-advocacy paper in five chapters, organised around five questions: what, why, current state, problems, and how.
- **Ch. 1** defines open source and the "AI open source ecosystem", citing OSI's 1998 definition, OSAID 1.0, the CAICT 2021 white paper and Stanford openness tiers.
- **Ch. 2** makes the strategic case at four levels:
  - national: technological sovereignty against a "technology monopoly structure", with a CUDA lock-in case;
  - local: industrial upgrading;
  - market: business models and one-person companies (OPCs);
  - talent.
- **Ch. 3** is the core:
  - a five-element model of the ecosystem;
  - a 2×2 typology (collaboration centralisation × governance intensity) giving four models: single-organisation-led, peripheral-ecosystem, standard-exploration and neutral-governance;
  - a 15-project map with licences;
  - city profiles of Beijing, Shanghai, Shenzhen, Hangzhou, Suzhou and Zhuzhou;
  - a five-axis China–US comparison.
- **Ch. 4** diagnoses problems:
  - an "industrial-project mindset" in government;
  - short-termism in firms;
  - university evaluation that ignores code;
  - a missing industry "middle layer";
  - IP and licence ambiguity;
  - "platforms and projects, but no community";
  - no neutral third parties;
  - weak foundational layers and dependence on US standards.
- **Ch. 5** recommends:
  - long-termism and patient capital;
  - firms and universities as "twin drivers";
  - restrained local governments that supply public goods (compute, data sandboxes, use cases);
  - ecosystem-health metrics;
  - independent foundations;
  - "development moderately ahead of governance".
- **Appendix:** a comparison table of the four models.

Central thesis: China leads in application-layer openness (open-weight models), but its ecosystem is dominated by single companies. It has "closed source at the foundation" (chips, compute, inference/training systems) and lacks the neutral, foundation-governed, standard-setting projects that make up about 40% of US high-impact projects. The book treats open source as industrial infrastructure and a route to self-reliance, not as a commons for its own sake.

The comparison frame is **exclusively China–US**. Europe is mentioned once, and the EU never.

## 3. Ten key findings for EU–China cooperation

1. **Europe is almost absent.** Europe gets one mention (preface: "market-driven open source ecosystems of the United States and Europe"). There is no mention of the EU, the EU AI Act, Mistral or any other European model, OpenEuler-style or Eclipse foundations, ETSI/CEN, or joint projects. This is itself a finding: in this Hangzhou/Datawhale policy discourse, the benchmark and rival is the US only.
2. **The governance benchmark is US foundations** (ASF, LF, CNCF), plus OSI's OSAID as the definitional baseline. These are global or US-domiciled bodies where EU actors are active. They are a possible neutral meeting ground, given that the book itself recommends deeper participation in "governance bodies of international communities" (4.5).
3. **None of the five Chinese model families releases pretraining data** (Table 2: Qwen, GLM, DeepSeek, MiniMax, Intern). Licences are permissive (Apache 2.0 / MIT / modified MIT). By the book's own reading of OSAID 1.0, these are open-weight, not open-source AI. This is relevant to the AI Act's open-source exemption debate (the book itself is silent on it).
4. **Self-reliance framing dominates.** Open source is "an important institutional instrument for China to re-establish technological sovereignty" and a hedge against "external technological constraints". This mirrors EU digital-sovereignty rhetoric, giving a shared vocabulary but also a source of friction.
5. **National policy anchors with dates:**
   - State Council AI Plus Opinions (Aug 2025): open source contribution evaluation, an "internationally influential" open source system;
   - MIIT+7 AI Plus Manufacturing action (Jan 2026): "world-leading open source and open ecosystem" by 2027;
   - 2026 Government Work Report: "supporting the development of AI open source communities";
   - MoE vocational open source majors (Dec 2025);
   - New Generation AI Development Plan (2017).
6. **Local plans with quantified 2027–2028 targets:**
   - Shanghai open source plan (Dec 2025): 1–2 international communities, 100 companies, 200+ projects, 3 million developers, "simultaneous global release";
   - Beijing Open Source Ecosystem Plan 2026–2028: full-stack in-house toolchain, RISC-V, a "Chinese Hugging Face";
   - Suzhou OPC targets.
   These are commitments and targets, not results (Methodology §4).
7. **Funding instruments are vouchers and guidance funds**, not grants to commons:
   - computing, corpus, model and data vouchers (Beijing, Shenzhen, Hangzhou, Suzhou);
   - Suzhou computing subsidy up to RMB 2m/yr, awards up to RMB 50m, youth fund cluster over RMB 1bn;
   - Shenzhen up to RMB 300m/yr for basic research;
   - Hangzhou open source contribution awards and ModelScope developer-centre subsidies.
   No figures on public money going to neutral open source foundations.
8. **Platform metrics (level C, self-reported):**
   - ModelScope: over 170k models, over 9k MCP services, users in over 200 countries (Mar 2026, via Baidu Baike);
   - Qwen: over 7m downloads and over 90k enterprise customers (May 2024, dated);
   - Doubao: over 170m MAU;
   - Beijing: over 200 registered models.
   Hugging Face is named as the international reference platform. Its French co-founder origin is not noted.
9. **Developer geography:** in Ant Group's mapping of about 120k developers of leading AI open source projects, the US has 37.4% and China 18.7%. No European share is reported, so the observatory should source the EU share from the same Ant/OpenDigger data (links to R18.2–18.3).
10. **Recommendations compatible with EU practice:**
    - independent foundations "independently of government administration";
    - ecosystem-health metrics including "international influence";
    - recognition of code contributions in academic evaluation;
    - contributor agreements and vulnerability-response baselines.
    These mirror the CHAOSS/OSPO/EU OSOR agenda and are natural cooperation hooks (OSPO practice, metrics, education), though the book does not propose any EU link.

Quality issues found:
- Citation mismatches:
  - Shanghai "Super Individual 288" is cited to [31], which is the Shenzhen plan;
  - Shenzhen RMB 300m is cited to [24] (Qwen 2.5 news; it should be [33]);
  - the 114-project analysis in 3.4.3 is cited to [50] (it should be [51]);
  - the Hangzhou "private enterprises ~90%" inline link goes to an nbd.com.cn article on Shenzhen.
- The AI Plus Manufacturing document is called both "Implementation Opinions" and "Implementation Plan".
- The book claims OSAID requires training data to be open. OSAID actually requires "data information".
- Table 2 simplifies Dify's and lobe-chat's licences, which add conditions to Apache 2.0.
